CHAPTER XXXIII.


After some opposition, Marianne yielded to her sister’s entreaties, and
consented to go out with her and Mrs. Jennings one morning for half an
hour. She expressly conditioned, however, for paying no visits, and
would do no more than accompany them to Gray’s in Sackville Street,
where Elinor was carrying on a negotiation for the exchange of a few
old-fashioned jewels of her mother.

When they stopped at the door, Mrs. Jennings recollected that there was
a lady at the other end of the street on whom she ought to call; and as
she had no business at Gray’s, it was resolved, that while her young
friends transacted their’s, she should pay her visit and return for
them.

On ascending the stairs, the Miss Dashwoods found so many people before
them in the room, that there was not a person at liberty to tend to
their orders; and they were obliged to wait. All that could be done
was, to sit down at that end of the counter which seemed to promise the
quickest succession; one gentleman only was standing there, and it is
probable that Elinor was not without hope of exciting his politeness to
a quicker despatch. But the correctness of his eye, and the delicacy of
his taste, proved to be beyond his politeness. He was giving orders for
a toothpick-case for himself, and till its size, shape, and ornaments
were determined, all of which, after examining and debating for a
quarter of an hour over every toothpick-case in the shop, were finally
arranged by his own inventive fancy, he had no leisure to bestow any
other attention on the two ladies, than what was comprised in three or
four very broad stares; a kind of notice which served to imprint on
Elinor the remembrance of a person and face, of strong, natural,
sterling insignificance, though adorned in the first style of fashion.

Marianne was spared from the troublesome feelings of contempt and
resentment, on this impertinent examination of their features, and on
the puppyism of his manner in deciding on all the different horrors of
the different toothpick-cases presented to his inspection, by remaining
unconscious of it all; for she was as well able to collect her thoughts
within herself, and be as ignorant of what was passing around her, in
Mr. Gray’s shop, as in her own bedroom.

At last the affair was decided. The ivory, the gold, and the pearls,
all received their appointment, and the gentleman having named the last
day on which his existence could be continued without the possession of
the toothpick-case, drew on his gloves with leisurely care, and
bestowing another glance on the Miss Dashwoods, but such a one as
seemed rather to demand than express admiration, walked off with a
happy air of real conceit and affected indifference.

Elinor lost no time in bringing her business forward, was on the point
of concluding it, when another gentleman presented himself at her side.
She turned her eyes towards his face, and found him with some surprise
to be her brother.

Their affection and pleasure in meeting was just enough to make a very
creditable appearance in Mr. Gray’s shop. John Dashwood was really far
from being sorry to see his sisters again; it rather gave them
satisfaction; and his inquiries after their mother were respectful and
attentive.

Elinor found that he and Fanny had been in town two days.

“I wished very much to call upon you yesterday,” said he, “but it was
impossible, for we were obliged to take Harry to see the wild beasts at
Exeter Exchange; and we spent the rest of the day with Mrs. Ferrars.
Harry was vastly pleased. _This_ morning I had fully intended to call
on you, if I could possibly find a spare half hour, but one has always
so much to do on first coming to town. I am come here to bespeak Fanny
a seal. But tomorrow I think I shall certainly be able to call in
Berkeley Street, and be introduced to your friend Mrs. Jennings. I
understand she is a woman of very good fortune. And the Middletons too,
you must introduce me to _them_. As my mother-in-law’s relations, I
shall be happy to show them every respect. They are excellent
neighbours to you in the country, I understand.”

“Excellent indeed. Their attention to our comfort, their friendliness
in every particular, is more than I can express.”

“I am extremely glad to hear it, upon my word; extremely glad indeed.
But so it ought to be; they are people of large fortune, they are
related to you, and every civility and accommodation that can serve to
make your situation pleasant might be reasonably expected. And so you
are most comfortably settled in your little cottage and want for
nothing! Edward brought us a most charming account of the place: the
most complete thing of its kind, he said, that ever was, and you all
seemed to enjoy it beyond any thing. It was a great satisfaction to us
to hear it, I assure you.”

Elinor did feel a little ashamed of her brother; and was not sorry to
be spared the necessity of answering him, by the arrival of Mrs.
Jennings’s servant, who came to tell her that his mistress waited for
them at the door.

Mr. Dashwood attended them down stairs, was introduced to Mrs. Jennings
at the door of her carriage, and repeating his hope of being able to
call on them the next day, took leave.

His visit was duly paid. He came with a pretence at an apology from
their sister-in-law, for not coming too; “but she was so much engaged
with her mother, that really she had no leisure for going any where.”
Mrs. Jennings, however, assured him directly, that she should not stand
upon ceremony, for they were all cousins, or something like it, and she
should certainly wait on Mrs. John Dashwood very soon, and bring her
sisters to see her. His manners to _them_, though calm, were perfectly
kind; to Mrs. Jennings, most attentively civil; and on Colonel
Brandon’s coming in soon after himself, he eyed him with a curiosity
which seemed to say, that he only wanted to know him to be rich, to be
equally civil to _him_.

After staying with them half an hour, he asked Elinor to walk with him
to Conduit Street, and introduce him to Sir John and Lady Middleton.
The weather was remarkably fine, and she readily consented. As soon as
they were out of the house, his enquiries began.

“Who is Colonel Brandon? Is he a man of fortune?”

“Yes; he has very good property in Dorsetshire.”

“I am glad of it. He seems a most gentlemanlike man; and I think,
Elinor, I may congratulate you on the prospect of a very respectable
establishment in life.”

“Me, brother! what do you mean?”

“He likes you. I observed him narrowly, and am convinced of it. What is
the amount of his fortune?”

“I believe about two thousand a year.”

“Two thousand a-year;” and then working himself up to a pitch of
enthusiastic generosity, he added, “Elinor, I wish with all my heart it
were _twice_ as much, for your sake.”

“Indeed I believe you,” replied Elinor; “but I am very sure that
Colonel Brandon has not the smallest wish of marrying _me_.”

“You are mistaken, Elinor; you are very much mistaken. A very little
trouble on your side secures him. Perhaps just at present he may be
undecided; the smallness of your fortune may make him hang back; his
friends may all advise him against it. But some of those little
attentions and encouragements which ladies can so easily give will fix
him, in spite of himself. And there can be no reason why you should not
try for him. It is not to be supposed that any prior attachment on your
side—in short, you know as to an attachment of that kind, it is quite
out of the question, the objections are insurmountable—you have too
much sense not to see all that. Colonel Brandon must be the man; and no
civility shall be wanting on my part to make him pleased with you and
your family. It is a match that must give universal satisfaction. In
short, it is a kind of thing that”—lowering his voice to an important
whisper—“will be exceedingly welcome to _all parties_.” Recollecting
himself, however, he added, “That is, I mean to say—your friends are
all truly anxious to see you well settled; Fanny particularly, for she
has your interest very much at heart, I assure you. And her mother too,
Mrs. Ferrars, a very good-natured woman, I am sure it would give her
great pleasure; she said as much the other day.”

Elinor would not vouchsafe any answer.

“It would be something remarkable, now,” he continued, “something
droll, if Fanny should have a brother and I a sister settling at the
same time. And yet it is not very unlikely.”

“Is Mr. Edward Ferrars,” said Elinor, with resolution, “going to be
married?”

“It is not actually settled, but there is such a thing in agitation. He
has a most excellent mother. Mrs. Ferrars, with the utmost liberality,
will come forward, and settle on him a thousand a year, if the match
takes place. The lady is the Hon. Miss Morton, only daughter of the
late Lord Morton, with thirty thousand pounds. A very desirable
connection on both sides, and I have not a doubt of its taking place in
time. A thousand a-year is a great deal for a mother to give away, to
make over for ever; but Mrs. Ferrars has a noble spirit. To give you
another instance of her liberality:—The other day, as soon as we came
to town, aware that money could not be very plenty with us just now,
she put bank-notes into Fanny’s hands to the amount of two hundred
pounds. And extremely acceptable it is, for we must live at a great
expense while we are here.”

He paused for her assent and compassion; and she forced herself to say,

“Your expenses both in town and country must certainly be considerable;
but your income is a large one.”

“Not so large, I dare say, as many people suppose. I do not mean to
complain, however; it is undoubtedly a comfortable one, and I hope will
in time be better. The enclosure of Norland Common, now carrying on, is
a most serious drain. And then I have made a little purchase within
this half year; East Kingham Farm, you must remember the place, where
old Gibson used to live. The land was so very desirable for me in every
respect, so immediately adjoining my own property, that I felt it my
duty to buy it. I could not have answered it to my conscience to let it
fall into any other hands. A man must pay for his convenience; and it
_has_ cost me a vast deal of money.”

“More than you think it really and intrinsically worth.”

“Why, I hope not that. I might have sold it again, the next day, for
more than I gave: but, with regard to the purchase-money, I might have
been very unfortunate indeed; for the stocks were at that time so low,
that if I had not happened to have the necessary sum in my banker’s
hands, I must have sold out to very great loss.”

Elinor could only smile.

“Other great and inevitable expenses too we have had on first coming to
Norland. Our respected father, as you well know, bequeathed all the
Stanhill effects that remained at Norland (and very valuable they were)
to your mother. Far be it from me to repine at his doing so; he had an
undoubted right to dispose of his own property as he chose, but, in
consequence of it, we have been obliged to make large purchases of
linen, china, &c. to supply the place of what was taken away. You may
guess, after all these expenses, how very far we must be from being
rich, and how acceptable Mrs. Ferrars’s kindness is.”

“Certainly,” said Elinor; “and assisted by her liberality, I hope you
may yet live to be in easy circumstances.”

“Another year or two may do much towards it,” he gravely replied; “but
however there is still a great deal to be done. There is not a stone
laid of Fanny’s green-house, and nothing but the plan of the
flower-garden marked out.”

“Where is the green-house to be?”

“Upon the knoll behind the house. The old walnut trees are all come
down to make room for it. It will be a very fine object from many parts
of the park, and the flower-garden will slope down just before it, and
be exceedingly pretty. We have cleared away all the old thorns that
grew in patches over the brow.”

Elinor kept her concern and her censure to herself; and was very
thankful that Marianne was not present, to share the provocation.

Having now said enough to make his poverty clear, and to do away the
necessity of buying a pair of ear-rings for each of his sisters, in his
next visit at Gray’s, his thoughts took a cheerfuller turn, and he
began to congratulate Elinor on having such a friend as Mrs. Jennings.

“She seems a most valuable woman indeed. Her house, her style of
living, all bespeak an exceeding good income; and it is an acquaintance
that has not only been of great use to you hitherto, but in the end may
prove materially advantageous. Her inviting you to town is certainly a
vast thing in your favour; and indeed, it speaks altogether so great a
regard for you, that in all probability when she dies you will not be
forgotten. She must have a great deal to leave.”

“Nothing at all, I should rather suppose; for she has only her
jointure, which will descend to her children.”

“But it is not to be imagined that she lives up to her income. Few
people of common prudence will do _that_ and whatever she saves, she
will be able to dispose of.”

“And do you not think it more likely that she should leave it to her
daughters, than to us?”

“Her daughters are both exceedingly well married, and therefore I
cannot perceive the necessity of her remembering them farther. Whereas,
in my opinion, by her taking so much notice of you, and treating you in
this kind of way, she has given you a sort of claim on her future
consideration, which a conscientious woman would not disregard. Nothing
can be kinder than her behaviour; and she can hardly do all this,
without being aware of the expectation it raises.”

“But she raises none in those most concerned. Indeed, brother, your
anxiety for our welfare and prosperity carries you too far.”

“Why, to be sure,” said he, seeming to recollect himself, “people have
little, have very little in their power. But, my dear Elinor, what is
the matter with Marianne?—she looks very unwell, has lost her colour,
and is grown quite thin. Is she ill?”

“She is not well, she has had a nervous complaint on her for several
weeks.”

“I am sorry for that. At her time of life, any thing of an illness
destroys the bloom for ever! Hers has been a very short one! She was as
handsome a girl last September, as I ever saw; and as likely to attract
the man. There was something in her style of beauty, to please them
particularly. I remember Fanny used to say that she would marry sooner
and better than you did; not but what she is exceedingly fond of _you_,
but so it happened to strike her. She will be mistaken, however. I
question whether Marianne _now_, will marry a man worth more than five
or six hundred a-year, at the utmost, and I am very much deceived if
_you_ do not do better. Dorsetshire! I know very little of Dorsetshire;
but, my dear Elinor, I shall be exceedingly glad to know more of it;
and I think I can answer for your having Fanny and myself among the
earliest and best pleased of your visitors.”

Elinor tried very seriously to convince him that there was no
likelihood of her marrying Colonel Brandon; but it was an expectation
of too much pleasure to himself to be relinquished, and he was really
resolved on seeking an intimacy with that gentleman, and promoting the
marriage by every possible attention. He had just compunction enough
for having done nothing for his sisters himself, to be exceedingly
anxious that everybody else should do a great deal; and an offer from
Colonel Brandon, or a legacy from Mrs. Jennings, was the easiest means
of atoning for his own neglect.

They were lucky enough to find Lady Middleton at home, and Sir John
came in before their visit ended. Abundance of civilities passed on all
sides. Sir John was ready to like anybody, and though Mr. Dashwood did
not seem to know much about horses, he soon set him down as a very
good-natured fellow: while Lady Middleton saw enough of fashion in his
appearance to think his acquaintance worth having; and Mr. Dashwood
went away delighted with both.

“I shall have a charming account to carry to Fanny,” said he, as he
walked back with his sister. “Lady Middleton is really a most elegant
woman! Such a woman as I am sure Fanny will be glad to know. And Mrs.
Jennings too, an exceedingly well-behaved woman, though not so elegant
as her daughter. Your sister need not have any scruple even of visiting
_her_, which, to say the truth, has been a little the case, and very
naturally; for we only knew that Mrs. Jennings was the widow of a man
who had got all his money in a low way; and Fanny and Mrs. Ferrars were
both strongly prepossessed, that neither she nor her daughters were
such kind of women as Fanny would like to associate with. But now I can
carry her a most satisfactory account of both.”

As they pulled up to the shop door, Mrs. Jennings suddenly remembered she owed a short social visit to a friend at the far end of the street, and as she had no business of her own at Gray’s, it was settled that she would slip away to make her call and return to collect the girls once their errand was done.

Climbing the stairs to the showroom, the Miss Dashwoods found the counters crowded with customers, and not a single clerk free to take their order. They were forced to wait, choosing a spot at the far end of one counter where only one very fashionably dressed gentleman stood lingering. Elinor held a quiet hope that he might hurry through his business out of courtesy to the two ladies waiting, but his eye for finery and his obsession with getting exactly what he wanted far outstripped any impulse to politeness. He was in the process of commissioning a custom toothpick case for himself, and for a full quarter of an hour he fussed over every ivory, gold, and pearl design in the shop, debating every last detail of size, shape, and ornament until he had mapped out the exact piece his own fancy had dreamed up. For the whole wait, he spared the sisters nothing more than three or four broad, unapologetic stares — a show of attention that branded him on Elinor’s memory as a man of pure, sterling insignificance, wrapped up in the very height of empty, fashionable vanity. Marianne, however, escaped all irritation at his rude gawking and his silly, childish devotion to such a trivial trinket: she was so deep in her own private, grieving thoughts, she was as oblivious to the world around her as if she was alone in her bedroom at Barton Cottage.

At last the order was settled. Every detail of the toothpick case had been approved, the gentleman named the latest possible date he could bear to go without the finished piece, drew on his gloves with lazy, deliberate care, tossed one more arrogant glance at the Miss Dashwoods that seemed to demand their admiration rather than offer any courtesy, and sauntered off with an air of unshakable self-conceit thinly masked by pretended indifference.

Elinor wasted no time stepping up to the counter to explain her own business, and was just on the cusp of wrapping up the negotiation when a second man stepped up beside her. She lifted her eyes to his face, and gasped softly in surprise to find it was her own brother, John Dashwood. Their pleasure at seeing one another was warm and genuine enough to make for a very sweet, respectable reunion in the middle of Gray’s crowded shop. John was genuinely glad to run into his sisters, and his inquiries after their mother were respectful and thoughtful. He explained he and Fanny had been in London for two days already.

“I fully meant to call on you yesterday,” he said, “but it was impossible — we had to take Harry to Exeter Exchange to see the wild beasts, and spent the rest of the day with Mrs. Ferrars. Harry was utterly delighted. This morning I swore I’d find half an hour to drop by, but the first days in town are always so crowded with errands. I’ve come here to order Fanny a new wax seal. But tomorrow I absolutely will call on you in Berkeley Street, and be introduced to your friend Mrs. Jennings. I hear she’s a woman of very considerable fortune. And you must introduce me to the Middletons, too — as relations of my stepmother, I shall be delighted to show them every proper respect. They’ve been excellent neighbors to you in the country, I understand?”

“More than excellent,” Elinor assured him. “Their care for our comfort, their endless kindness, is more than I can ever properly thank them for.”

“I’m overjoyed to hear it, truly I am,” he nodded, satisfied. “And it’s only right, isn’t it? They’re people of great wealth, related to you through your father’s first family, so every civility that could make your life easier was only to be expected. Edward told us the loveliest stories of your little cottage, said it was the coziest, most perfect little place of its kind he’d ever seen, and that all of you seemed happier there than anywhere else. It was a great comfort to us to hear it, I assure you.”

Elinor felt a faint flush of embarrassment, and was relieved to be spared the need to reply when Mrs. Jennings’ servant appeared at the shop door to say his mistress was waiting for them by the carriage. John walked them all down the stairs, was formally introduced to Mrs. Jennings by the carriage step, repeated his promise to call on them the next day, and took his leave.

He arrived promptly the next day, bearing an apologetic excuse from Fanny, who could not join them: she was far too busy attending to her own mother’s affairs to step out, he said. Mrs. Jennings waved off all formality at once, insisting they were practically cousins, and she would certainly call on Mrs. John Dashwood very soon, bringing the Dashwood sisters with her. John’s manners to Elinor and Marianne were calm but perfectly kind; to Mrs. Jennings, they were unfailingly civil and attentive, and when Colonel Brandon stepped through the front door shortly after he did, John eyed the older man with such sharp curiosity it was obvious he was mentally tallying up his fortune, ready to match his civility to whatever sum he found.

After half an hour of chat, he asked Elinor to walk with him to Conduit Street, to introduce him properly to Sir John and Lady Middleton. The day was uncommonly fine, so she agreed readily. The moment they stepped out of the house, his questions spilled out.

“Who exactly is Colonel Brandon? Is he a man of good fortune?”

“Yes,” Elinor said. “He has a very fine estate in Dorsetshire, bringing in a very steady income.”

“I’m delighted to hear it! He seems the very picture of a gentleman, and Elinor — I must congratulate you on the prospect of a very respectable, comfortable establishment for life.”

“Me? Brother, whatever do you mean?”

“He likes you! I watched him very closely, and I’m entirely convinced of it. What did you say his total income was?”

“About two thousand a year, I believe.”

“Two thousand a year!” John’s face lit up with a performative, over-the-top air of generous delight. “Elinor, with all my heart I wish it was twice as much, for your sake.”

“Thank you, I truly believe you mean that,” Elinor replied, “but I am completely certain Colonel Brandon has not the slightest wish to marry me.”

“You’re mistaken, Elinor, very much mistaken. A very small amount of gentle encouragement on your part would secure him at once. He might be wavering right now, of course — the smallness of your fortune might make him hesitate, his friends might all advise against the match. But those little, soft attentions that ladies know so well how to give will fix him, no matter what reservations he has. There’s no reason at all you shouldn’t try. I don’t imagine you have any lingering prior attachment — in short, you know that kind of old, ill-fated infatuation is completely out of the question, the obstacles are insurmountable, and you have more than enough sense to see that. Colonel Brandon is the perfect match for you, and I will make every effort to be as civil to him as I can, to make him feel welcome to our family. It’s a match everyone will be overjoyed by. In fact —” he dropped his voice to an important, excited whisper “— it will be exceedingly welcome to all parties.” He paused, correcting himself quickly. “That is, your friends are all so anxious to see you well settled — Fanny most of all, she has your best interests entirely at heart, I promise you. And Mrs. Ferrars, Fanny’s mother, is such a kind woman, she said just the other day how happy that match would make her.”

Elinor refused to dignify that with a reply.

“It would be a most remarkable, droll little coincidence, wouldn’t it,” he went on, “if Fanny’s brother and my own sister were to settle and marry at exactly the same time. And it’s not even all that unlikely!”

“Is Mr. Edward Ferrars,” Elinor asked, steady and deliberate, “soon to be married?”

“It’s not formally settled yet, but it’s all well in hand. His mother is the most generous woman alive — Mrs. Ferrars has promised to settle a full thousand a year on him, if the match goes through. The lady is the Honourable Miss Morton, only daughter of the late Lord Morton, with thirty thousand pounds of her own. It’s a perfect, desirable connection for both sides, and I have no doubt at all it will happen soon. A thousand a year is no small sum for a mother to give away permanently, but Mrs. Ferrars has a most noble, generous spirit. Just think — the other day, the very moment we arrived in town, knowing we were sure to be a little short on funds after moving into Norland, she pressed two hundred pounds worth of bank notes straight into Fanny’s hands. It was such a welcome gift, for living in town is extraordinarily expensive for us right now.”

He paused, waiting for her agreement and sympathy, and Elinor forced herself to say, “Your expenses both in town and at Norland must be very considerable, but your income is a very large one, after all.”

“Not nearly as large as people assume,” he sighed. “I don’t mean to complain, of course — it’s a very comfortable income, and I hope it will grow better with time. But the enclosure of Norland Common that’s going on right now has been a massive drain on our funds. And then I made a small purchase earlier this year — East Kingham Farm, you must remember the place where old Gibson used to live. The land was so perfectly situated right next to our own property, I felt it was my duty to buy it, I couldn’t in good conscience let it fall into someone else’s hands. Convenience always costs a price, and that farm cost me a very great deal of money.”

“More than it was intrinsically worth, I expect,” Elinor said.

“Oh, I hope not! I could have turned around and sold it the very next day for more than I paid. But when it came to the purchase money, I was very nearly very unlucky — the stocks were so low at the time, if I hadn’t happened to have the full sum sitting with my banker already, I would have had to sell out my shares and take a terrible loss.”

Elinor could only smile faintly. “We had other great, unavoidable expenses right after moving into Norland, too,” he continued. Our respected father, as you well know, left all the remaining Stanhope household goods at Norland — and they were very valuable — to your mother. Far be it from me to complain about that, he had every right to dispose of his property as he chose. But because of that, we had to replace almost all the linen, the china, every last household item he gave away. You can imagine, after all these costs, how far we are from being well off, and how grateful we were for Mrs. Ferrars’s kindness.”

“Of course,” Elinor said. “With her generous support, I hope you will soon be comfortably well situated.”

“Another year or two will see to a great deal of that,” he said gravely. “But there is still so much more to do. We haven’t even laid a single stone for Fanny’s new greenhouse yet, and all we have of the new flower garden is a marked out plan.”

“Where is the greenhouse to be built?”

“On the knoll behind the house. We cut down all the old walnut trees there to make space for it. It will be a stunning feature to look at from all across the park, and the new flower garden will slope down right in front of it, so it will be exceedingly pretty. We cleared away all the ugly old thorn bushes that used to grow all over the brow of that hill.”

Elinor kept her dismay and her quiet censure to herself, and was very thankful Marianne was not there to share the provocation of hearing all their old Norland family trees cut down for a frivolous new garden.

Now that he had made very clear just how “strapped” he was for cash, and neatly eliminated any chance of him offering to buy his sisters a pair of ear-rings the next time he visited Gray’s, his mood brightened, and he began gushing over how lucky Elinor was to have a friend like Mrs. Jennings.

“She seems an incredibly valuable woman! Her house, her whole way of living, makes it obvious she has a very large fortune. This acquaintance has already been so useful to you, and I’m sure in the end it will prove even more materially advantageous. Her inviting you up to town was such a great favour to you, and she is so openly fond of you, it’s almost certain you and Marianne will not be forgotten in her will. She must have a great deal of money left to leave.”

“I should think not very much at all,” Elinor said. “All she has is her jointure, which is bound to go to her daughters.”

“But no woman of reasonable prudence spends every penny of her income, now, does she?” he argued. “Whatever she saves up over the years, she can dispose of however she likes.”

“Surely it’s far more likely she’ll leave those savings to her own daughters, rather than to us?”

“Her two daughters are already very comfortably married, there’s no need to leave them anything more. Whereas, in my opinion, she has treated you with such extraordinary kindness, she has given you a sort of claim on her future generosity that no conscientious woman could ignore. Her behaviour to you has been perfectly warm, and she can’t possibly be that kind without being aware of the hopes it raises.”

“But neither Marianne nor I hold any such hopes. Brother, your concern for our well being is making you see things that are not there.”

“Of course, well, people have very little power over who gets what, at the end of the day,” he said, as if recalling himself. “But my dear Elinor — what is the matter with Marianne? She looks very unwell, her colour is all gone, and she’s grown so thin. Is she ill?”

“She’s not well. She’s had a nervous complaint plaguing her for several weeks now.”

“I am sorry to hear that. At her age, any sort of lingering illness ruins a girl’s bloom forever! Hers was such a short one, too. Just last September she was the prettiest girl I ever saw, the kind that was sure to catch a gentleman’s eye. Fanny used to say, you know, that Marianne would marry sooner and better than you. Not that she isn’t very fond of you, of course, that’s just what she thought. But she’ll be wrong now. I doubt Marianne will ever marry a man with more than five or six hundred a year, at the very most, but I am very sure you will do far better. Dorsetshire! I don’t know much of Dorsetshire, but my dear Elinor, I will be so delighted to come visit you there, and I can promise Fanny and I will be the first and happiest of your guests.”

Elinor tried very seriously to convince him there was no chance at all of her marrying Colonel Brandon, but the fantasy was far too pleasing to John for him to let it go. He was already fully determined to cultivate a close friendship with the Colonel, and push the match forward with every show of attention. He had just enough leftover guilt for never doing a single thing to help his sisters himself, that he was desperate for everyone else to do the work for him — an offer from Colonel Brandon, or a nice legacy from Mrs. Jennings, was the easiest possible way to make up for his own neglect.

They were lucky enough to find Lady Middleton at home, and Sir John walked in before their visit was over. Courtesies were exchanged all around, Sir John was ready to like anyone, and even though John Dashwood knew next to nothing about horses, he quickly decided he was a very good natured fellow. Lady Middleton, meanwhile, saw more than enough fashionable polish in his appearance to decide his acquaintance was well worth having. John left the Middletons’ home absolutely delighted with both of them.

“I shall have the most charming report to carry back to Fanny,” he told Elinor as they walked home. “Lady Middleton is the very picture of elegant refinement! Fanny will be so glad to make her acquaintance. And Mrs. Jennings, too, she’s so perfectly well behaved, even if she is not quite as elegant as her daughter. Fanny had some small scruples about visiting her, you know, and very naturally — we only knew her as the widow of a man who made all his money in very low trade, and Fanny and Mrs. Ferrars were both fully convinced neither she nor her daughters were the sort of women Fanny would care to associate with. But now I can bring home a perfectly satisfactory account of both of them.”
